title: Three more families that misbehave
goal: Read roots that begin with י, end with א, or end with a guttural.

sections.body: The three families in the last lesson cover most of what goes wrong. These three cover nearly all the rest — and between them they account for a startling share of the commonest verbs in the language.

item.why: The initial י will not stand at the head of a syllable in the future, so it drops and the prefix vowel lengthens to cover the gap.

forms.label: he will sit
forms.note: the root yod is gone; the prefix carries a tsere

forms.label: to sit
forms.note: an infinitive with no yod in it at all

item.why: The final א stopped being pronounced, so the vowel before it stretches and the endings attach as though it were not there.

forms.label: I found
forms.note: the א is written and never heard

forms.label: he will find
forms.note: a patach, where the strong verb has a cholam

item.en: roots ending in ע or ח
item.why: A final ע or ח cannot close a syllable on any vowel but a, so an extra a-sound slides in underneath it — the furtive patach.

forms.label: he hears
forms.note: the patach is heard before the ע, not after

forms.label: he will hear
forms.note: patach again, where כתב takes a cholam

sections.body: None of these is irregular in the English sense. Each is the ordinary pattern bending around a letter that will not take the vowel the pattern asks for — ע and ח will not close a syllable on anything but an a, א stops being pronounced at all, and a י at the head of a word turns into a vowel. Knowing which letter is causing the trouble is most of reading the form.

That is the last of the grammar the verb system needs. What remains is the habit of looking at an unfamiliar verb and asking three questions in order: which three letters are the root, which binyan is this shape, and which tense are those prefixes.

exercises.q: How do you say “to sit, to live somewhere”?
